DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# OPENING: Christ had no human biological father

**Position.** Jesus Christ had no human biological father. Mary conceived by the Holy Ghost, not by Joseph or any man. Joseph was the husband of Mary and the one who named the child, but he did not beget him.

## 1. The text says the conception was before any union

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** *Synelthein* (G4905, "to come together") is the word behind "came together." The pregnancy is dated before that coming together. *Ek* (G1537, "out of," marking source) stands in "of the Holy Ghost": *ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** *Gennēthen* (G1080 *gennaō*, "to beget, to conceive") is passive. The child is begotten in her, and the source is again *ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of the Holy Ghost."

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 puts the conception before Mary and Joseph came together. Matthew 1:20 names the Holy Ghost as the source (*ek*) of what was begotten in her. So the verses give no human male source for the child.

## 2. Matthew's genealogy breaks its own pattern at the end

**[L1]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob." **[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Every "begat" in the list is *egennēsen* (G1080), active: the man begat. At the last step the verb changes to *egennēthē* (G1080, "was born," passive). The relative "of whom" is *ex hēs* ("out of whom"), feminine singular, which points to Mary and not to Joseph. The text calls Joseph "the husband of Mary," not the one who begat Jesus.

**[L4]** The active "begat" runs through the whole genealogy, and the last link carries a passive verb and a feminine relative instead. Two lexical facts (the voice change and the feminine *hēs*) plus the verse's own wording show Jesus is traced out of Mary and not out of Joseph.

## 3. Mary's question and the answer

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (G1097, "to know") is the word for marital knowledge. *Anēr* (G435, "man, husband") is the one she has not known.

**[L3]** Genesis 4:1: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain." Here *yada* (H3045, "to know") is the marital idiom, and conception follows it. In Luke 1:34 she has not had that knowledge.

**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L4]** Mary's "I know not a man" (Luke 1:34, *ginōskō*) and the angel's answer (Luke 1:35) fit together. The conception comes from the Holy Ghost coming upon her, not from a man. Genesis 4:1 shows that "knew" is the word for the act that otherwise yields conception, and in Luke 1:34 that act has not taken place.

## 4. The prophecy and its fulfilment

**[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L2]** The Hebrew behind KJV "virgin" is *almah* (H5959), a maiden. The KJV renders it "virgin," and I rest on the KJV's word.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:22-23: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."

**[L2]** *Parthenos* (G3933, "virgin") stands in Matthew 1:23. **[L1]** Luke 1:27 uses the same word for Mary: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph."

**[L4]** Matthew 1:22 says the conception was "done" so as to fulfil Isaiah 7:14. Matthew 1:23 carries the word "virgin" (*parthenos*), and Luke 1:27 applies that word to Mary before the conception. So the text presents her as a virgin when she conceived.

## 5. Joseph did not father him

**[L1]** Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."

**[L2]** *Apolysai* (G630, "to release, put away") is what Joseph was minded to do when he found her with child (Matthew 1:18).

**[L4]** Joseph decided to put away a wife found with child. That decision stands on Matthew 1:18, where the pregnancy came before they came together, and on Matthew 1:20, where the angel has to tell him the child is "of the Holy Ghost." Had he known himself the cause, he would have had no reason to put her away, and the angel would have had nothing to explain. Joseph's reaction therefore marks him as not the father.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (G1097, "to know") is the same marital word as in Luke 1:34. Joseph did not know her until the child was born.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:25 (no knowing before the birth) and Matthew 1:18 (pregnancy before coming together) rule out Joseph as begetter. His part is to take her and give the name (Matthew 1:20, 1:24-25). That is a legal act and not a begetting.

## 6. "Father" in the text

**[L1]** Luke 2:48: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." **[L1]** Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

**[L4]** Mary says "thy father" of Joseph, and the child answers with "my Father's business." He puts the Father's claim above that of Joseph. Luke 1:35 gives the ground: he "shall be called the Son of God" because the Holy Ghost came upon Mary.

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (G3543 *nomizō*, "to reckon, to suppose") marks Joseph's fatherhood as a supposition. **[L3]** John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" That is what the murmuring crowd said, and Luke 3:23 sets the narrator's qualification beside it.

**[L1]** Hebrews 10:5: "but a body hast thou prepared me."

**[L2]** *Katērtisō* (G2675 *katartizō*, "to fit, to prepare") says the body was prepared, and the verse names God as the one who prepared it.

**[L4]** Luke 3:23 marks "son of Joseph" as supposed, and Hebrews 10:5 says the body was prepared by God. Together they show that statements calling Joseph his father (Luke 2:48, John 6:42) report what people reckoned, not who begat him.

## DECLARED CHAIN

1. The conception predated Mary and Joseph coming together, and its source is the Holy Ghost: Matthew 1:18 and Matthew 1:20 [L1]; *synelthein* ("to come together") and *ek* ("out of," source) [L2]; chain: pregnancy before union plus a named source other than a man leaves no human male source in the text.
2. Matthew's genealogy turns from the active "begat" to the passive "was born... of whom," and ties Jesus to Mary and not to Joseph: Matthew 1:2 and Matthew 1:16 [L1]; *egennēsen* (active "begat") against *egennēthē* (passive "was born") and feminine *ex hēs* ("out of whom") [L2].
3. Mary had not known a man, and "knowing" is the word for the act that yields conception: Luke 1:34 and Luke 1:35 [L1]; *ginōskō* ("to know") and *anēr* ("man") [L2]; Genesis 4:1 [L3] shows "knew" followed by conception, so Mary's not knowing a man excludes any man's seed.
4. The text calls Mary a virgin at conception and Joseph's fatherhood a supposition: Isaiah 7:14, Matthew 1:23, Luke 1:27 and Luke 3:23 [L1]; *almah* (the maiden, rendered "virgin"), *parthenos* ("virgin") and *enomizeto* ("was supposed") [L2]; Matthew 1:22 [L3] states that the virgin conception was done to fulfil the prophecy.
5. Joseph did not know Mary before the birth and was minded to put her away: Matthew 1:19 and Matthew 1:25 [L1]; *apolysai* ("to put away") and *ginōskō* ("to know") [L2]; Matthew 1:20 [L3] has the angel explain the child's source to him, which he needed only because he was not the cause.
6. Answer to the topic: Christ had no human biological father. He was conceived of the Holy Ghost, Joseph was not his begetter, and God is his Father: Matthew 1:18, Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35 [L1]; *ek pneumatos hagiou* ("out of the Holy Ghost") and *katartizō* ("to prepare," a body prepared for him) [L2]; Luke 2:49 and Hebrews 10:5 [L3].

=== [CR2] ===
DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 2, RESPONSE

# LINK ROUND

I answer each listed premise by exhibiting its footing and meeting each pressed verse on its meaning. I make no claim that God's fatherhood is a bodily seed like a man's. My claim is narrower: no man's seed is the source of the child, and the text gives him a different source and a different ground for the title "Son of God."

---

## LINK 1: SUPPORTED

**Footing.** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
- **[L2]** *synelthein* (G4905, "to come together") and *heurethē* (G2147 *heuriskō*, "to find, discover").
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]"
- **[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate; figuratively, to regenerate").
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:20 also says Joseph "thought on these things."
- **[L2]** *enthymeomai* (G1760, "to ponder").
- **[L4]** Matthew 1:18 gives the source (*ek*, "out of," the Holy Ghost) in the same sentence that records the finding. Joseph "found" the pregnancy (G2147) and "thought on these things" (G1760). Both are the acts of a man confronted with a fact he did not expect. The angel's "for" then grounds "fear not" in the begotten child's source. A man who had known his betrothed would have no discovery to ponder and no fear to answer.

**Press: John 1:13.** "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."
- **[L2]** *haima* (G129, "blood"), *thelēma* (G2307, "will"), *anēr* (G435, "man").
- **[L4]** This verse sets "of God" against "of the will of man" in one sentence. In the *gennaō* pattern, "of God" is the source that replaces the human source. The press helps link 1.

**Press: 1 John 5:1.** "Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God: and every one that loveth him that begat loveth him also that is begotten of him."
- **[L2]** The lexicon glosses G1080 as "figuratively, to regenerate."
- **[L1]** John 1:13 speaks of believers' second birth ("born... of God").
- **[L4]** *ek* with *gennaō* in believers names a regeneration. Believers also had a separate birth in the flesh, and that is the birth John 1:13 sets aside. Matthew 1:20 speaks of what is "conceived in her," in a womb (G1064 *gastēr*, "womb," in Matthew 1:18's "with child"), dated "before they came together." It is a conception, not a regeneration. The press needs a birth in the flesh that precedes a spiritual one, and Matthew 1:18-20 gives one conception only.

**Press: Matthew 1:24, Deuteronomy 20:7.** Matthew 1:24: "and took unto him his wife." Deuteronomy 20:7: "And what man [is there] that hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her?"
- **[L2]** I grant that Matthew 1:24's taking is a taking home (G3880 *paralambanō*, "to receive near"), and that Deuteronomy 20:7 distinguishes betrothing from taking.
- **[L4]** On the challenger's own timing, any knowing falls before the taking, inside the espousal. Matthew 1:18 puts the finding of the child there as well. The Holy Ghost is named as the source at that finding, in a verse that dates the child before the taking. If Joseph had known her, the discovery, the pondering and the fear of Matthew 1:19-20 would have no cause. The press does not reach the source stated in 1:18, 1:20.

---

## LINK 2: SUPPORTED

**Footing.** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren."
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- **[L2]** *egennēsen* (G1080, active, "begat") for the man's act. *egennēthē* (G1080, passive, "was born") at the last step, with *hēs* (feminine, "whom").
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:18, the next verse: "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise."
- **[L4]** The verb and relative change at the last step. Matthew 1:18 then opens an explanation of how the birth came about. The genealogy's close is explained by the narrative that follows. The grammar by itself ties Jesus to Mary. Links 1 and 5 carry the exclusion of Joseph, and this link carries the break.

**Press: Matthew 11:11.** "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist."
- **Press: Job 14:1.** "Man [that is] born of a woman [is] of few days, and full of trouble."
- **Press: Galatians 4:4.** "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."
- **Press: Luke 1:13.** "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John."
- **[L2]** *gennētos* (G1084, "they that are born") is the form in Matthew 11:11. *ginomai* (G1096, "to become, come into being") is "made" in Galatians 4:4.
- **[L4]** I grant that "born of women" is the common lot, and I do not rest on that phrase. Luke 1:13 says "shall bear thee a son," so the angel names the husband as the one to whom the son is borne. Matthew 1:16 names Joseph only as "the husband of Mary." Galatians 4:4 says "his Son, made of a woman." The verb is "made" (*ginomai*), and the Son is the subject who comes to be of a woman.

**Davidic line, pressed through Luke 1:27, 1:5, 1:36.**
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:16 gives Joseph's father as Jacob, who "begat Joseph." Luke 3:23 gives "Joseph, which was [the son] of Heli," with "the son" in italics.
- **[L2]** *egennēsen* (G1080, "begat") stands in Matthew. Luke 3:23 has no begetting verb.
- **[L4]** One Joseph has two fathers named, and only the first is stated as a begetting. Luke's "of Heli" is therefore a reckoning that is not Joseph's begetting. A line of David through the woman's side fits both rows. Joseph's house enters the child's reckoning by the taking and the naming (Matthew 1:21, 1:24).

---

## LINK 3: SUPPORTED

**Footing.** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
- **[L2]** *pōs* (G4459, "in what way? how"). *ginōskō* (G1097, "to know"). *anēr* (G435, "man").
- **[L3]** Genesis 4:1: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain."
- **[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- **[L4]** Mary asks about the manner (*pōs*) of a conception. The angel answers the manner: the Holy Ghost and the power. Her question had to be answered by naming a means other than a man's knowing, because "knowing" is the stated means of conception in Genesis 4:1.

**Press: Luke 1:34 and Luke 1:31.** Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son." I grant that *ginōskō* is present tense and the conception is future.
- **[L1]** Luke 1:27: "a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph."
- **[L4]** If the conception were to come by Joseph after the taking, her espousal (Luke 1:27) would already have answered her "how." The question would then have no occasion. She asks "how," and the angel's reply gives the Holy Ghost's coming and the Highest's power. The present-tense reading supports my chain.

**Press: Luke 1:35 with Acts 1:8 and Luke 9:34.** Acts 1:8: "after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you." Luke 9:34: "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them."
- **[L2]** *eperchomai* (G2064 *erchomai*, "to come, go") and *episkiazō* (overshadow).
- **[L4]** I do not need these verbs to mean begetting. I need them to be the answer to "how shall this be," a question about conception. The answer is the Holy Ghost's coming and the Highest's overshadowing. These are acts of God at the place of Mary's womb, and no man's act is named in them.

**Press: the "therefore" back to Luke 1:32.** Luke 1:32: "He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest."
- **[L4]** Luke 1:35 reads "the Holy Ghost shall come upon thee... therefore also that holy thing... shall be called the Son of God." The "therefore" has the Holy Ghost's coming as its antecedent inside the same verse. The "also" adds the ground to the title already given in 1:32.

**Press: Luke 1:36 and Luke 1:13.** Luke 1:36: "thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age... who was called barren."
- **[L1]** Luke 1:37: "For with God nothing shall be impossible."
- **[L2]** *steira* (G4723, "barren").
- **[L4]** The sign shows God doing what nature had closed. It is introduced by "also." It does not make the two conceptions the same.

---

## LINK 4: SUPPORTED

**Footing.** Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."
- **[L2]** *parthenos* (G3933, "a maiden; an unmarried daughter").
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:22: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled."
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- **[L4]** Matthew 1:23 puts the virgin as the one who is with child. Matthew 1:25 keeps the not-knowing to the birth. So she was a virgin when she conceived.

**Press: Luke 1:27 and Deuteronomy 22:23.** Luke 1:27: "a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph." Deuteronomy 22:23: "If a damsel [that is] a virgin be betrothed unto an husband, and a man find her in the city, and lie with her."
- **[L2]** *shakab* (H7901, "to lie down, for sexual connection").
- **[L4]** I grant the espoused virgin is called a wife. Deuteronomy 22:23 places "a virgin... betrothed" before the lying with her. This is the state Matthew 1:23 names for the one who is "with child."

**Press: Isaiah 7:14 with Exodus 2:8, Psalm 68:25 and Proverbs 30:19.** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son." Exodus 2:8: "the maid went and called the child's mother." Psalm 68:25: "the damsels playing with timbrels." Proverbs 30:19: "the way of a man with a maid."
- **[L2]** *almah* (H5959, "maiden"), the word at Isaiah 7:14.
- **[L1]** The KJV's English at Isaiah 7:14 is "virgin," and Matthew 1:23 renders it with G3933 *parthenos*. In the press rows the woman is a maid or damsel, not a married woman.
- **[L1]** Isaiah 7:14 says "the Lord himself shall give you a sign."
- **[L2]** *'oth* (H226, "sign").
- **[L4]** A conception within an ordinary marriage is no sign. The KJV English stands.

**Press: Isaiah 7:16, 8:3, 8:4, 8:8.** Isaiah 8:3: "And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son. Then said the LORD to me, Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz." Isaiah 8:4: "before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother." Isaiah 8:8: "O Immanuel." Isaiah 7:16: "before the child shall know to refuse the evil."
- **[L4]** The child of Isaiah 8:3 receives the name Mahershalalhashbaz, not Immanuel. Isaiah 8:8's "O Immanuel" is spoken to the land. Matthew 1:22-23 takes Isaiah 7:14 as the word fulfilled in this birth: "they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."

**Press: Luke 3:23 with Acts 16:13 and Luke 2:48.** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." Acts 16:13: "where prayer was wont to be made." Luke 2:48: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."
- **[L2]** *enomizeto* (G3543 *nomizō*, "to reckon, suppose"). I grant it is from *nomos* (G3551, "law, prescriptive usage").
- **[L4]** At Acts 16:13 the place of prayer is a place held to be one. The KJV renders Luke 3:23 "as was supposed," and a supposition marks a reckoning. If Joseph were the begetter, Luke would have no need for it.
- **[L1]** Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" The child answers Mary's "thy father" with "my Father's."
- **[L1]** Luke 2:33: "And Joseph and his mother marvelled." Luke 2:43: "Joseph and his mother knew not of it."
- **[L2]** *goneis* (G1118, "parents").
- **[L4]** The same narrator who writes "his parents" in Luke 2:41 writes "Joseph and his mother" at Luke 2:33, 2:43. "Parents" does not by itself carry a begetting.

---

## LINK 5: SUPPORTED

**Footing.** Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."
- **[L2]** *apolysai* (G630, "to release, put away"), *dikaios* (G1342, "just"), *paradeigmatisai* (G3856, "to make a public example of").
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
- **[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- **[L4]** Joseph's grounds are his justness and his mercy, and I grant them. They act on a pregnancy he found, and he feared to take her. The angel's "for" answers that fear with the source of what was conceived.

**Press: Deuteronomy 22:24.** "the man, because he hath humbled his neighbour's wife... ye shall bring them both out unto the gate of that city."
- **[L2]** *ra'a* (H7453, "neighbour, fellow").
- **[L4]** The gate-case the challenger brings is of a betrothed woman and "the man" who "humbled his neighbour's wife," that is, another man's wife. If that is the background of Joseph's "public example," Joseph is the neighbour wronged, and the other man is the supposed cause. The press supports link 5.

**Press: Matthew 1:20 with 2 Samuel 7:14.** 2 Samuel 7:14: "I will be his father, and he shall be my son."
- **[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080, margin "begotten") is the verb of the angel's ground.
- **[L4]** The angel's ground uses the verb of begetting and names the source ("of the Holy Ghost"). Nothing in that ground quotes the covenant formula. The ground is what Joseph needed in order not to fear: where the child came from.

---

## LINK 6: SUPPORTED

**Footing.** Matthew 1:18, 1:20 and Luke 1:35, as in links 1 and 3.
- **[L1]** Hebrews 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me."
- **[L2]** *katartizō* (G2675, "to fit, prepare").
- **[L4]** The source is stated: the Holy Ghost. The ground of the title is stated: the Holy Ghost's coming ("therefore"). The body is stated as prepared. The link needs nothing more than that no man's seed is the source.

**Press: Romans 1:3-4.** "which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh; And declared [to be] the Son of God with power... by the resurrection from the dead. [declared: Gr. determined]"
- **[L2]** *ginomai* (G1096, "to become") is "made," not *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate"). *sperma* (G4690, "seed... by implication, offspring").
- **[L3]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman."
- **[L4]** The Son is the subject, and he "was made" of David's seed. The verb is the same as in "made of a woman," not "begat." The sperma is offspring: lineage.
- **[L1]** Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh."
- **[L3]** Hebrews 7:10: "For he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him." Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren."
- **[L2]** *osphys* (G3751, "loins").
- **[L4]** Hebrews 7:10 puts Levi in Abraham's loins, across the begettings of Matthew 1:2. "Loins" language spans generations. David's "fruit... according to the flesh" can run through Mary without a man's seed at the last step.
- **[L1]** Luke 1:32: "the throne of his father David." The angel calls David the child's "father" in the same chapter in which Mary asks "how." "Father" is a lineal word here, and it does not prove that "thy father" in Luke 2:48 is a begetter.

**Press: Psalm 2:7, Acts 13:33, Hebrews 5:5, Hebrews 1:5.** Psalm 2:7: "this day have I begotten thee." Acts 13:33: "in that he hath raised up Jesus again." Hebrews 1:5: "I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son."
- **[L4]** I grant that the begotten-row is applied to resurrection and priesthood. That shows God's "begotten" is not a bodily seed, which I do not claim. At Luke 1:35 the Son-title is grounded in the Holy Ghost's coming, before birth. At Romans 1:4 it is "declared" with power by the resurrection. The two moments do not conflict.

**Rows given: 1 Chronicles 28:6 and 2 Samuel 7:12, 14.** 1 Chronicles 28:6: "I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father."
